claims.claim: Some megakaryocytes resemble 'reservoirs' containing dozens of neutrophils in stages 2 and 3 of emperipolesis.
claims.source: While most MKs engaged in emperipolesis contained only one or two neutrophils, some resembled 'reservoirs' containing dozens of neutrophils in stages 2 and 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), an appearance recognized in human marrow as well (Cashell and Buss, 1992; Larsen, 1970; Monteferrario et al., 2014; Thiele et al., 1984) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Microscopy observations with reference to published literature (Cashell and Buss, 1992; Larsen, 1970; Monteferrario et al., 2014; Thiele et al., 1984).

claims.claim: Neutrophil transit through megakaryocytes can last more than one hour.
claims.source: Live cell imaging of murine MKs co-incubated with fresh bone marrow cells showed that neutrophil transit was of variable duration, in some cases lasting only a few minutes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and Videos 2, 3 and 5) and in others more than one hour (Video 6).
claims.evidence: Live cell imaging data shown in Video 6.

claims.claim: Megakaryocytes were observed to contain B220+ B cells, CD115+ monocytes, CD3+ T cells and NK1.1+ NK cells in addition to neutrophils.
claims.source: Neutrophils were by far the most common participants, although B220+ B cells, CD115+ monocytes, and occasional CD3+ T cells and NK1.1+ NK cells were also observed within MKs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Emperipolesis was observed in megakaryocytes cultured from marrow CD34+ cells but not from cord blood CD34+ cells.
claims.source: and was observed in MKs cultured from marrow CD34+ cells but not from the even smaller MKs derived from cord blood CD34+ cells (Figure 1D and not shown).
claims.evidence: Experimental observations from human MK cultures.

claims.claim: Megakaryocytes develop a complex network of intracytoplasmic membrane termed the demarcation membrane system (DMS) that provides a membrane reservoir to enable platelet generation.
claims.source: Mature MKs develop a complex network of intracytoplasmic membrane, termed the demarcation membrane system (DMS), that provides a membrane reservoir to enable platelet generation (Schulze et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Reference to published literature (Schulze et al., 2006).

claims.claim: Megakaryocytes protrude pseudopodial extensions of membrane via the marrow sinusoids into the bloodstream, where shear stress releases fragments that become mature platelets.
claims.source: MKs then protrude pseudopodial extensions of this membrane via the marrow sinusoids into the bloodstream, where shear stress releases fragments that become the mature platelets required for hemostasis (Junt et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Reference to published literature (Junt et al., 2007).

claims.claim: Developing megakaryocytes undergo multiple rounds of endomitosis to become highly-polyploid cells averaging 20 to 100 μm in size.
claims.source: Derived from hematopoietic stem cells, developing MKs undergo multiple rounds of endomitosis to become highly-polyploid cells averaging 20 to 100 μm in size (Levine et al., 1982; Machlus and Italiano, 2013).
claims.evidence: Reference to published literature (Levine et al., 1982; Machlus and Italiano, 2013).

claims.claim: Emperipolesis has been speculated to represent a sanctuary for neutrophils in an unfavorable marrow environment or a route for neutrophils to exit the bone marrow.
claims.source: It has been speculated that MKs could represent a sanctuary for neutrophils in an unfavorable marrow environment, or a route for neutrophils to exit the bone marrow, but more typically emperipolesis is regarded as a curiosity without physiological significance (Lee, 1989; Sahebekhitiari and Tavassoli, 1976; Tavassoli, 1986).
claims.evidence: Reference to published speculations (Lee, 1989; Sahebekhitiari and Tavassoli, 1976; Tavassoli, 1986).

claims.claim: Emperipolesis is typically regarded as a curiosity without physiological significance.
claims.source: It has been speculated that MKs could represent a sanctuary for neutrophils in an unfavorable marrow environment, or a route for neutrophils to exit the bone marrow, but more typically emperipolesis is regarded as a curiosity without physiological significance (Lee, 1989; Sahebekhitiari and Tavassoli, 1976; Tavassoli, 1986).
claims.evidence: Reference to published literature (Lee, 1989; Sahebekhitiari and Tavassoli, 1976; Tavassoli, 1986).

claims.claim: Megakaryocytes have a direct role in systemic inflammation.
claims.source: Recently, we identified evidence for a direct role for MKs in systemic inflammation, highlighting the potential importance of the interaction of MKs with immune lineages (Cunin and Nigrovic, 2019; Cunin et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Reference to authors' prior published work (Cunin and Nigrovic, 2019; Cunin et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Emperipolesis is strikingly heterogeneous in terms of megakaryocyte size, number of neutrophils, and duration.
claims.source: Emperipolesis is nevertheless strikingly heterogeneous. For example, emperipolesis can be observed in MKs of all sizes and can last just minutes to over an hour. MKs may enclose a single neutrophil or encompass as many as 50 neutrophils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Synthesis of observations from multiple experiments.

claims.claim: There may be different types of emperipolesis, involving different molecular pathways and serving distinct functions.
claims.source: These observations strongly suggest that there may be different types of emperipolesis, involving different molecular pathways and serving distinct functions that remain to be defined.
claims.evidence: Inference from observed heterogeneity in emperipolesis.

claims.claim: Emperipolesis is a tightly-regulated process mediated actively by both megakaryocytes and neutrophils via pathways reminiscent of leukocyte transendothelial migration.
claims.source: We show here that emperipolesis is a tightly-regulated process mediated actively by both MKs and neutrophils via pathways reminiscent of leukocyte transendothelial migration.
claims.evidence: Synthesis of experimental findings on molecular mechanisms.

claims.claim: Neutrophils enter megakaryocytes within membrane-bound vesicles but then penetrate into the cell cytoplasm where they develop membrane continuity with the demarcation membrane system to transfer membrane to megakaryocytes and thereby to platelets.
claims.source: Neutrophils enter MKs within membrane-bound vesicles but then penetrate into the cell cytoplasm, where they develop membrane continuity with the demarcation membrane system (DMS) to transfer membrane to MKs and thereby to platelets, accelerating platelet production.
claims.evidence: Synthesis of microscopy and membrane labeling experiments.

claims.claim: Neutrophils emerge intact from megakaryocytes carrying megakaryocyte components with them.
claims.source: Neutrophils then emerge intact, carrying MK components with them.
claims.evidence: Inference from live cell imaging and membrane labeling experiments.

claims.claim: Emperipolesis mediates a novel form of material transfer between immune and hematopoietic lineages.
claims.source: Together, these data identify emperipolesis as a previously unrecognized type of cell-in-cell interaction that mediates a novel form of material transfer between immune and hematopoietic lineages.
claims.evidence: Synthesis of all experimental findings.

results.result: Emperipolesis occurs in vivo in murine and human marrow, with approximately 6% of murine MKs containing at least one neutrophil. In vitro, murine MKs exhibit efficient emperipolesis (20-40%), while human MKs show lower efficiency (2-5%). Neutrophils are the predominant cell type, though other immune cells also participate.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5, C85-C86 provide converging quantitative evidence from multiple imaging modalities (whole-mount 3D immunofluorescence, confocal microscopy) in both murine and human systems. The data are internally consistent and supported by appropriate figures showing direct visualization of the phenomenon.

results.result: Emperipolesis proceeds through distinct stages: neutrophils enter MKs within CD41+ membrane-bound vacuoles (emperisomes), the vacuolar space is resorbed leading to membrane apposition, and ultimately only a single membrane separates neutrophil from MK cytoplasm. Transit duration is highly variable, ranging from minutes to over an hour.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10, C59, C83-C84 are supported by complementary evidence from live cell imaging, confocal microscopy, and electron microscopy. The multi-stage process is well-documented with temporal resolution and ultrastructural detail. The heterogeneity in duration is directly observed.

results.result: Emperipolesis requires active actin polymerization by both MKs and neutrophils. Neutrophils exhibit polarized morphology during entry, while MKs develop transcellular cups similar to those in transendothelial migration. Actin localizes to the MK-neutrophil interface and encases CD41+ vacuoles but not intracytoplasmic neutrophils.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C16, C58, C95 are supported by pharmacological inhibition studies (latrunculin A, cytochalasin D), immunofluorescence localization, and comparison to established biological processes. The bidirectional requirement is demonstrated by treating either cell type separately. Controls for inhibitor effects are provided.

results.result: Emperipolesis is mediated in part by neutrophil β2 integrin (CD18) binding to MK ICAM-1, with ezrin serving as a cytoskeletal linker. Blockade or genetic deficiency of these components partially impairs emperipolesis, indicating involvement of additional unidentified mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C25, C79-C80, C82 are supported by multiple complementary approaches: blocking antibodies, knockout mice, pharmacological inhibition, and co-localization studies. The partial impairment with each intervention consistently indicates mechanistic redundancy. Negative controls (C79) strengthen the specificity of the findings.

results.result: Neutrophils transfer membrane to MKs via emperipolesis through membrane contiguity with the DMS. This transfer is demonstrated by loss of lipid dye fluorescence from intracellular neutrophils and is actin-dependent. Reciprocal membrane transfer from MKs to neutrophils occurs primarily via MK microparticles, not emperipolesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C37 are supported by electron microscopy showing membrane contiguity, multiple independent lipid labeling experiments, time-lapse microscopy, and differential sensitivity to latrunculin A. The bidirectional nature and distinct mechanisms are well-established through complementary approaches including supernatant controls.

results.result: Membrane transfer from neutrophils to MKs includes surface proteins, as demonstrated by detection of biotin on MKs after co-culture with biotinylated marrow cells. However, biotin is not detected on platelets produced by MKs co-cultured with biotinylated marrow cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39, C46 are supported by surface biotinylation experiments with appropriate controls. The detection of biotin on MKs but not on platelets is internally consistent and suggests selective protein transfer or dilution effects during platelet production.

results.result: Neutrophil membrane and intracellular proteins are transferred to platelets produced by MKs that underwent emperipolesis. This occurs both in adoptive transfer experiments and in chimeric mice with native marrow environment. The transferred membrane persists on platelets over time.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C45, C47-C48, C61 are supported by multiple independent labeling approaches (CellVue Maroon, PKH67, mT/mG, CellTrace Violet) in both adoptive transfer and chimeric mouse models. The consistency across different experimental systems and labeling methods provides strong evidence. Time-course data demonstrate persistence of transferred material.

results.result: A substantial fraction of emperipolesis-derived platelets in chimeric mice express phosphatidylserine while maintaining normal CD62P levels and tubulin organization. This suggests these platelets may be functionally distinct with potentially enhanced thrombogenic capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 provide observational data on phosphatidylserine expression with appropriate controls. However, C51 is explicitly speculative about functional consequences. While C76 establishes the biological significance of phosphatidylserine, actual functional testing of these platelets (e.g., coagulation assays, thrombosis models) is absent. The result requires additional validation.

results.result: Emperipolesis frequency increases approximately 2-fold (from ~2-5% to ~6-10%) in murine models of inflammation (LPS, IgG-mediated thrombocytopenia). However, enhanced platelet production drive alone (TPO, anti-CD41) is insufficient to augment emperipolesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53, C63 are supported by quantitative histological analysis across multiple stress models with appropriate controls. The differential response to inflammatory versus proliferative stimuli is well-documented and suggests specific regulatory mechanisms. Sample sizes appear adequate for the observed effect sizes.

results.result: Emperipolesis enhances platelet production both in vitro and in vivo. Co-culture with live marrow cells increases pro-platelet formation compared to MKs cultured alone, with fixed cells, or with supernatants. MKs co-cultured with marrow cells produce more platelets in adoptive transfer experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56, C64 are supported by complementary in vitro (IncuCyte) and in vivo (adoptive transfer) approaches with appropriate controls. The use of fixed cells and supernatants effectively rules out contact-independent and soluble factor mechanisms. Statistical significance is reported for key comparisons.

results.result: Neutrophils exit MKs intact and viable after emperipolesis, carrying MK components with them. This distinguishes emperipolesis from phagocytosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C62, C71, C97 are supported by live cell imaging showing viable neutrophil egress and bidirectional membrane transfer experiments. The distinction from phagocytosis is well-established through demonstration of active neutrophil participation, survival, and exit.

results.result: Emperipolesis represents a novel cell-in-cell interaction mediating material transfer between immune and hematopoietic lineages, enabling modulation of platelet production and membrane content.
results.evaluation: Claims C72, C98 represent synthesis conclusions supported by the totality of experimental findings. The novelty is justified by the unique combination of features: bidirectional material transfer, viable cell exit, and functional consequences for platelet production. This integrates multiple major findings into a coherent biological framework.

results.result: Background context on MK biology, emperipolesis in disease states, evolutionary conservation, and comparison to transendothelial migration based on published literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C92 are appropriately cited references to established literature providing context. These are not novel findings but rather background information supporting the rationale and interpretation of the current work. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.

results.result: Emperipolesis exhibits substantial heterogeneity in MK size, neutrophil number, and duration, suggesting multiple types of emperipolesis with potentially distinct molecular pathways and functions.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 is well-supported by observational data showing variability. However, C94's inference about multiple distinct types is speculative. While heterogeneity is clearly demonstrated, whether this reflects fundamentally different processes versus a continuum of the same process remains unproven. Additional mechanistic dissection would be needed.

results.result: Emperipolesis may enable MKs to 'groom' neutrophils and other immune lineages through bidirectional material transfer.
results.evaluation: Claim C78 is explicitly speculative, based on inference from bidirectional membrane transfer and viable cell exit. While the observations support the possibility, no functional data demonstrate actual 'grooming' effects on neutrophil phenotype or function. This represents a hypothesis for future investigation rather than an established result.
